title: Marriage, Singleness, and Staying Where God Called You
summary: Answering questions the Corinthians had sent him, Paul affirms mutual sexual obligation within marriage, forbids divorce between believers (citing the Lord), and permits separation when an unbelieving spouse leaves. He urges each person to remain in the situation in which God called them, and commends singleness as a gift that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord, while insisting that those who marry do not sin.
story: With the words “Now for the matters you wrote about” (verse 1), the letter changes gear. Chapters 1 to 6 responded to reports Paul had heard; from here to chapter 16 he mostly answers the church's own letter, and several sections open with the formula “now about” (7:1, 7:25, 8:1, 12:1, 16:1, 16:12). Chapter 6 had warned against sexual immorality; here Paul addresses the opposite error, a view that even married sex was unspiritual. The chapter's governing principle, remain as you were called (verses 17 to 24), keeps both the ascetic and the libertine from treating their circumstances as the measure of their holiness, and it looks ahead to the end of the age, “the time is short” (verse 29), a theme that returns in chapter 15.
historical:
Paul writes around AD 53 to 55 from Ephesus. Some ancient sources mention grain shortages in parts of the eastern Mediterranean during the 40s and 50s, and some scholars connect the “present crisis” of verse 26 with such hardship in Corinth; others read the phrase as the distress that marks the whole period between Christ's resurrection and his return. Either way, Paul's advice about marrying is shaped by conditions he considered pressing, and he says openly that it is his judgment, not a command from the Lord (verses 6, 25, and 40).

Roman society pushed people toward marriage. Laws issued under the emperor Augustus penalized unmarried adults and rewarded those who had children, and widows and divorcées of child-bearing age were expected to remarry. Against that pressure, Paul's commendation of singleness would have sounded countercultural; against the ascetic party in Corinth, his insistence that marriage is no sin sounded equally so.
cultural:
In Roman law either spouse could end a marriage simply by leaving with the intent to divorce; there was no court procedure and no clear distinction between separating and divorcing. That is why Paul uses the words interchangeably in verses 10 to 15. Marriages were usually arranged by families, girls were often married in their mid to late teens, and a father or guardian had a large say, which lies behind the debated verses 36 to 38.

Circumcision (verses 18 and 19) was the mark of Jewish identity; some Jewish men in the Greek world had surgery to hide it in order to take part in the gymnasium, and some Gentile converts felt pressure to be circumcised. Slavery (verses 21 to 23) was woven through Roman society; estimates vary, but a large share of the people in a city like Corinth were slaves or former slaves, and freeing slaves (manumission) was common. Paul uses both conditions to show that a person's social standing is not what makes them acceptable to God.
literary: The chapter is a series of answers, each built on a similar pattern: a general principle, an exception or concession, and a reason. Paul carefully marks the authority behind each ruling: a command from the Lord (verse 10, echoing Jesus's teaching on divorce), his own apostolic word (verse 12), and his considered judgment (verses 25 and 40). The section on remaining as called (verses 17 to 24) sits at the center and repeats its refrain three times (verses 17, 20, 24). Balanced pairs run throughout (husband and wife, wife and husband), so that every obligation is mutual, an unusual feature for ancient moral writing on marriage.

outline.t: Remain in the situation in which you were called
About virgins: the short time and undivided devotion

doctrines.note: Marriage is honored and bound by obligation in both directions: husband and wife each have a claim on the other (verses 3 and 4). Singleness is also honored as a gift from God (verse 7), not a failure or a lesser state. Both are callings to serve the Lord.

A believing spouse “sanctifies” an unbelieving partner and makes the children “holy” (verse 14). This does not mean they are saved automatically, but that the household is not defiled by the unbeliever and the marriage stands under God's claim.

“This world in its present form is passing away” (verse 31). Paul does not despise marriage, grief, joy, or property, but he asks believers to hold them loosely because they belong to an age that is ending.

words.note: Charisma, a gift of grace. The same word Paul uses for spiritual gifts in chapter 12 is used here for both marriage and singleness: “each man has his own gift from God” (verse 7). Neither state is a spiritual achievement; each is a gift to be used.

Kaleo, to call, used nine times here. For Paul, calling is God's summons to belong to Christ, not primarily a career or a role. The command to remain as called means that one's social situation (married, single, slave, free, circumcised or not) is the place to serve God, not a barrier to be escaped first.

Chorizo, to separate. In Greek legal usage this was a normal word for divorce, since leaving a marriage was the act that ended it. Paul uses it for the wife who separates (verses 10 and 11) and for the unbeliever who leaves (verse 15).

Amerimnos, free from concern or anxiety. Paul wants believers to be free of anxious distraction (verse 32), and argues that the unmarried person can more easily give undivided attention to the Lord. It is practical advice about focus, not a claim that married people are less holy.

christ: Paul explicitly passes on a teaching of Jesus: “To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord)” (verse 10), echoing Jesus's words on divorce preserved in Mark 10:2-12 and Matthew 19:3-9. The whole chapter assumes that believers belong to Christ first: the slave is “the Lord's freedman,” the free man is “Christ's slave” (verse 22), and all were “bought at a price” (verse 23). Paul's own singleness serves Christ's mission, and his advice to hold this world loosely comes from the conviction that Christ's return and the new age have drawn near. Christ is the center that relativizes every earthly status, whether marriage, rank, or ethnicity.

hard.q: What does this chapter permit about divorce and remarriage, and what did Paul mean by the “virgin” in verses 36 to 38?
hard.a:
On divorce, Paul repeats Jesus's prohibition for two believers (verses 10 and 11), adding that a wife who separates should remain unmarried or be reconciled. For a believer married to an unbeliever, he forbids the believer to initiate divorce but says that if the unbeliever leaves, “the believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases” (verse 15). Christians have read this differently. Many Protestants have taken “not bound” to mean the believer is free to remarry, which with Matthew's exception for sexual immorality gives two grounds for divorce and remarriage (a view found in the Westminster Confession). Others hold that “not bound” means only freed from the duty to keep the marriage together, and that remarriage while the former spouse lives is not permitted, a position closer to Roman Catholic teaching and to some Protestant traditions. Faithful churches differ, and pastoral care in real cases has always needed wisdom beyond a single verse.

Verses 36 to 38 are also debated. Most modern translations, including this one, take them to describe an engaged man deciding whether to marry his betrothed. An older reading, reflected in the King James Version, takes the man to be a father deciding whether to give his virgin daughter in marriage, which fits the verb in verse 38 (literally to give in marriage). A third, less common view imagines a couple living together in a spiritual, celibate marriage. On every reading, Paul's point is the same: marrying is not sin, and not marrying for the Lord's sake is also good.

questions: Paul calls both marriage and singleness a gift from God. How might a church honor single people as fully as it honors married couples and families?
What does it mean in practice to remain in the situation in which God called you, and when is it right to change it (verse 21)?
How would your use of time, money, and relationships change if you really believed that “this world in its present form is passing away”?
